newsitem.title: USA: Cuban officials testify in Miami court case.
newsitem.headline: Cuban officials testify in Miami court case.

text.p: A Cuban intelligence officer and three border guards made a highly unusual appearance in a Miami court to testify about a cocaine seizure on a Colombian freighter off Cuba's coast, legal sources said on Friday.

The four wore civilian clothes for their district court appearance on Thursday in a city with a huge Cuban exile community that is for the most part virulently opposed to the government of Cuban President Fidel Castro.
They testified in the trial of the captain and chief engineer of the freighter Limerick in a case that gave rise to a rare show of cooperation between the Cuban and U.S. governments.

Capt. Francisco Williams-May and engineer Arcadio Archbol-Wilson were arrested in October along with about a dozen crewmen by U.S. Coast Guard officers who boarded the ship after it began to sink in international waters off Cuba's coast near the U.S. military base at Guantanamo.

The stricken ship, which had been sailing from Baranquilla, Colombia, to Freeport in the Bahamas, then drifted into Cuba's waters where Cuban officials boarded it and allegedly found a haul of cocaine.

Cuban intelligence officer Lt. Col. Freddy Curbeno testified in court that he ordered boats to the scene in response to a request from the U.S. Coast Guard. He said he accompanied 69 bales discovered on board from Santiago de Cuba to Havana.
The bales, which the prosecution says contained cocaine, were later flown to Miami after the two sides agreed to cooperate. The detained men were brought up from the U.S. base in Guantanamo.
The four Cuban officials were accompanied by a U.S. diplomat from the U.S. Interests Section in Havana.

Law enforcement officials say such cooperation between the two avowed enemies is unusual but not unprecedented. In December prosecutors from Tampa flew to Cuba to interview relatives of an alleged hijacker and two Miami detectives went to Havana in October in connection with a murder allegedly committed by a Cuban refugee.
Cuba's cooperation in the Limerick case was praised by Washington in its annual International Narcotics Control Strategy report.
But Florida Congressman Lincoln Diaz-Balart accused Washington of covering up what he said was Castro's involvement in the drugs trade.

"The real story behind this sad case of collaboration between the U.S. Administration and the Cuban tyranny is the cover up of proof of Castro's particpation in narco-trafficking," he said in a statement.
In Havana, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Marianela Ferriol said: "Cuba is always willing to cooperate in the fight against drug trafficking."
Cuba has said in the past that it would be prepared to have a formal anti-drugs cooperation agreement with the United States but that Washington opposes this for political reasons.
